title: Iceland Cuts Electric-Car Grant and Lowers Price Ceiling From 1 November
dek: The passenger-car grant falls from ISK 500,000 to ISK 400,000, and cars priced above ISK 8 million no longer qualify. Support for vans and buses continues for businesses.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Electric cars plugged into public charging points

keyPoints: From November 1, the grant for eligible electric passenger cars falls by ISK 100,000, from ISK 500,000 to ISK 400,000.
The maximum price of an eligible passenger car falls from ISK 10 million to ISK 8 million.
The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate announced the change on October 14.
Support for vans, goods vehicles and buses continues, limited to companies and people actively operating a business.
body:
Iceland has reduced its purchase grant for electric passenger cars from November 1, and has lowered the price ceiling for eligible vehicles, according to Iceland Review.

## What changed

The grant falls from ISK 500,000 to ISK 400,000. The maximum price of an eligible car drops from ISK 10 million to ISK 8 million, so cars costing more than ISK 8 million no longer qualify. Vans, goods vehicles and buses remain eligible, but only for companies and people actively operating a business.

## The government's reasoning

The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate announced the change on October 14. The ministry says the lower ceiling is meant to direct support toward less expensive cars, and argues that earlier grants largely benefited higher-income buyers. It also says falling electric-car prices have changed the case for direct subsidies.

The change comes with a new framework for the Climate and Energy Fund. Buyers should check the fund's detailed conditions before committing to a purchase, since the ministry's announcement does not by itself establish an individual vehicle's eligibility.

## Charging is a separate question

The grant covers vehicle purchases, not access to chargers. Iceland Review has recently reported plans for 21 additional charging stations outside the capital area, and earlier coverage has examined slower electric-vehicle sales and registrations.
